title: Sic Bo in Canada: A 2026 Guide to the Dice Game
excerpt: How Sic Bo works, what every bet on the layout actually costs you, and why Small and Big beat the flashy 180:1 triples. A clear guide for Canadian players.
author: Lisa Davids
bodyHtml:
Sic Bo is the loudest-looking table in the casino and one of the simplest games in it. Three dice, one shaker, a grid of numbers, and a round that is over in seconds. The game traces back to ancient China, travelled to Macau and then to Western casino floors, and now sits in the lobby of almost every Canadian-facing site in both software and live-dealer form. Playing online Sic Bo in Canada takes about thirty seconds to learn. Playing it well takes understanding the paytable, because the difference between the cheapest bet on the layout and the most expensive one is enormous, and nothing on screen warns you which is which.

How a round of Sic Bo works

Three standard six-sided dice sit inside a shaker or a small mechanical dome. Players place chips on a betting layout covered in totals, pairs, triples and individual numbers. When betting closes, the dice are shaken and revealed. Every bet is then settled instantly against the three faces showing, winners are paid per the posted paytable, and the layout clears for the next round.

There is no decision after the roll. No hitting, no standing, no doubling. Unlike blackjack or video poker, Sic Bo has no strategy that unfolds during a hand, so the whole of your influence over the result happens before the dice move. That makes bet selection the only skill on offer. If you are still comparing table games generally, our casino games hub lays out where dice games sit alongside the rest of the lobby.

The main Sic Bo bets and what they actually cost

Three dice produce 216 equally likely combinations. Every bet on the layout is a slice of those 216 outcomes, priced at something less than fair odds. The gap between the true probability and the payout is the house edge, and on this layout it ranges from modest to genuinely punishing.

Small, Big, Even and Odd

Small wins on a total of 4 through 10. Big wins on a total of 11 through 17. Both pay even money, and both lose on any triple, which is the mechanism that gives the house its cut. That produces a house edge of roughly 2.78 per cent, comfortably the best number on the table. Even and Odd work the same way, paying even money, losing on triples, and landing at about the same 2.78 per cent.

Totals

You can bet the exact sum of the three dice, from 4 up to 17. The extreme totals are rare and pay accordingly. A total of 4 or 17 commonly returns 60:1. Middling totals like 10 or 11 come up far more often and typically pay around 6:1, with house edges frequently sitting in the 12.5 per cent range. Edges on total bets swing considerably depending on which number you pick and which paytable the studio uses, and two Sic Bo tables can price the same total differently.

Triples, doubles and combinations

The eye-catching bets live here. A specific triple, three fours for example, usually pays 180:1 and carries a house edge of around 16.2 per cent. Any triple, meaning all three dice match on any face, typically pays 30:1 with an edge near 30.1 per cent, which makes it one of the most expensive wagers on any casino table anywhere. A specific double pays about 10:1 for an edge around 18.5 per cent. Two-dice combinations, where you nominate two different faces and need both to appear, generally pay 5:1 at roughly a 16.7 per cent edge.

Single numbers

Pick a face from one to six. If it shows on one die you are paid 1:1, on two dice 2:1, and on all three 3:1. The edge lands around 7.9 per cent. It is not the cheapest bet available, but it is far kinder than the exotics and it keeps you involved in most rolls.

Ranked from cheapest to most expensive, the layout looks roughly like this:

  • Small, Big, Even and Odd, around 2.78 per cent
  • Single number bets, around 7.9 per cent
  • Total bets, commonly around 12.5 per cent but highly variable by number
  • Specific triple at 180:1, around 16.2 per cent
  • Two-dice combinations at 5:1, around 16.7 per cent
  • Specific double at 10:1, around 18.5 per cent
  • Any triple at 30:1, around 30.1 per cent

Paytables vary, and that is the real lesson

Sic Bo has no single standardised paytable. Different providers and live studios price the same wager differently, and a bet that looks identical on two layouts can carry an edge several percentage points apart. A total of 9 paying 6:1 is a meaningfully worse bet than the same total paying 7:1.

So before you sit down, open the rules panel and read the actual payouts. It takes a minute and it is the most valuable habit in this game. The pattern holds almost universally: Small, Big, Even and Odd are consistently the cheapest bets, and the high-payout exotics are consistently the most expensive.

Dice have no memory

Live Sic Bo tables often display a history of recent totals, and RNG versions sometimes do the same. It looks like data. It is not. Each roll is independent of every roll before it, so a total that has not appeared in fifty rounds is exactly as likely on the next roll as it was on the first. Tracking hot numbers or waiting for a triple that feels due has no mathematical basis.

The related trap is progressive staking. Martingale systems, where you double after every loss, look bulletproof on paper and fail in practice for two reasons: table maximums cut the sequence short, and a run of losses long enough to break you is not remotely unusual on even-money bets. Flat stakes are duller and considerably safer. This is the same misreading that trips people up across the lobby, as our look at the most searched online casino games in Canada shows in game after game.

Live dealer Sic Bo versus RNG Sic Bo

RNG Sic Bo is software. You control the pace, rounds resolve instantly, stakes usually start very low, and it is ideal for learning the layout without pressure. Live-dealer Sic Bo streams in real time from a studio, with a human host or an automated shaker, fixed round timers and a shared table of players. The maths is the same in both formats; the experience is not.

Some live studios layer random multipliers onto selected bets each round, which can turn a modest win into a large one. Read the fine print, because that upside is usually funded by a reduced base paytable somewhere else on the layout. A multiplier feature is a repricing of the game, not free money.

Playing in Canada, on mobile and within your limits

Sic Bo appears on Ontario-regulated sites and on Alberta's regulated market as well as at international operators serving Canadians, and live tables stream to phones as readily as to desktops. The layout is dense, so a decent mobile build matters more here than in most games; our guide to the best mobile casinos in Canada covers which apps handle live tables cleanly.

Decide your session budget before the first roll and your stake per round after that, ideally one to two per cent of that budget. Set a time limit as well as a money limit, because rounds resolve in seconds and Sic Bo burns through a bankroll quickly. Stick to Small, Big, Even and Odd if longevity is the goal, treat the 180:1 triples as an occasional small-stake flutter rather than a plan, and never chase a losing session.
